B.1: Every year, the I R S forces retirees to pull money out of their I R A, whether they need it or not. It is called a required minimum distribution, and every dollar of it is taxable. Walter is seventy-five, and this year he must take out thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty dollars. But one move, allowed by the I R S, can cut his tax bill by more than two thousand dollars. Here are the exact numbers, step by step.
B.2: Meet two people. Walter is seventy-five, single, with eight hundred thousand dollars in a traditional I R A and thirty thousand dollars a year from Social Security. Linda turns seventy-three this year, with five hundred thousand dollars in her I R A, and she is about to face her very first required distribution. Walter will show us how the tax works, and Linda will show us the deadline trap that catches new retirees.
B.3: Every number in this video comes from the Internal Revenue Service: Publication five ninety-B on I R A distributions, the I R S questions and answers on required minimum distributions, Form fifty-three twenty-nine, and Publication nine fifteen on Social Security taxes. No news articles, no guesses. Every example follows the exact steps printed on the I R S forms. Let's start with who has to take this money out.
B.4: Part one: the basics. You must start required minimum distributions the year you reach age seventy-three. The rule applies to traditional I R As, and to workplace plans like a four oh one K. But a Roth I R A has no required distributions while you are alive, and neither does a designated Roth account in a workplace plan. So this rule hits traditional money only. Everything else in this video is about that traditional money.
B.5: Here is the formula, straight from the I R S. Take your account balance on December thirty-first of last year, and divide it by a life expectancy factor from the Uniform Lifetime Table. At seventy-three the factor is twenty-six point five. At seventy-five it is twenty-four point six. At eighty it is twenty point two. At eighty-five it is sixteen. At ninety it is twelve point two. The factor keeps shrinking, so the share you must take keeps growing.
B.6: Now Walter. His I R A was worth eight hundred thousand dollars on December thirty-first. He is seventy-five, so his factor is twenty-four point six. Eight hundred thousand divided by twenty-four point six is thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty dollars. That is about four percent of the account, and it is his minimum for this year. He can take more, but never less.
B.7: Now Linda, who turns seventy-three this year. Her I R A had five hundred thousand dollars at the end of last year, and her factor is twenty-six point five. Five hundred thousand divided by twenty-six point five is eighteen thousand eight hundred sixty-eight dollars. That is her first required distribution. And here is the surprise: the I R S gives her until April first of next year to take it.
B.8: That extra time is a trap. After the first year, every distribution is due by December thirty-first. So if Linda waits until April, she takes two distributions in the same year. Suppose her balance grows to five hundred ten thousand dollars, and her next factor is twenty-five point five. That second one is twenty thousand dollars. Together: thirty-eight thousand eight hundred sixty-eight dollars of taxable income in a single year.
B.9: Next, the penalty. If you take less than the required amount, the I R S charges an excise tax of twenty-five percent on the amount you did not take out. For Walter, missing the whole thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty dollars would cost eight thousand one hundred thirty dollars. If you fix it in time, the rate drops to ten percent, which is three thousand two hundred fifty-two dollars. You report it on Form fifty-three twenty-nine, and you can ask for a waiver if the mistake was reasonable.
B.10: Now the part nobody explains. A required distribution is taxable income, and it also pulls your Social Security into the tax. The I R S adds half of Walter's Social Security, fifteen thousand dollars, to his thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty dollar distribution. That makes forty-seven thousand five hundred twenty dollars, far above the thirty-four thousand dollar line for a single person. Above that line, up to eighty-five percent of his benefits can be taxed.
B.11: Using the I R S worksheet in Publication nine fifteen, fifteen thousand nine hundred ninety-two dollars of Walter's Social Security is taxable. Add his distribution, and his income on the return is forty-eight thousand five hundred twelve dollars. His deductions, from our last video, are twenty-four thousand one hundred fifty, so he is taxed on twenty-four thousand three hundred sixty-two. His federal income tax: two thousand six hundred seventy-five dollars.
B.12: Now the move. It is called a qualified charitable distribution, or Q C D. You send money directly from your I R A to a charity, and that amount is not counted as income. You must be at least seventy and a half, which is earlier than seventy-three. The limit is one hundred eight thousand dollars for twenty twenty-five, and one hundred eleven thousand for twenty twenty-six, per person. And a Q C D counts toward your required minimum distribution.
B.13: Let's say Walter already gives to his church and his local charities, and he sends ten thousand dollars straight from his I R A. His taxable I R A income drops from thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty to twenty-two thousand five hundred twenty. Now the worksheet gives only seven thousand four hundred ninety-two dollars of taxable Social Security. His income on the return falls to thirty thousand twelve dollars, and he is taxed on only five thousand eight hundred sixty-two.
B.14: His federal income tax falls from two thousand six hundred seventy-five dollars to five hundred eighty-six dollars. That is two thousand eighty-nine dollars saved. And the share of his Social Security that is taxed drops from fifty-three percent to twenty-five percent. Be honest about the trade: the ten thousand dollars goes to charity, so this works best when you already planned to give. The same gift from a bank account would not lower his income the same way.
B.15: Now the rules that trip people up. The money must go directly from your I R A trustee to the charity, never through your own pocket first. It works from a traditional I R A, but not from an ongoing SEP or SIMPLE I R A. You need a written receipt, just like any donation. You cannot also deduct that gift. And on Form ten forty, you enter only the part that is still taxable on line four B, and mark the Q C D box on line four C.
B.16: Two more rules can prevent a mistake. If you own several I R As, you calculate the required amount for each one separately, but you can withdraw the total from any one of them. A four oh one K or a four fifty-seven B is different: each plan must pay its own required amount. And if you are still working, you can delay the amount from your current employer's plan until the year you retire, unless you own five percent of the company. That exception does not cover I R As.
B.17: When you take money out of a traditional I R A, the I R S default is that ten percent is withheld for federal tax, unless you choose otherwise. You can fill out Form W four R to pick a different rate, so the tax is paid as you go and April holds no surprise. If too little is withheld, you may need to pay estimated tax during the year. And remember, if you take more than the minimum in one year, the extra cannot be counted toward the next year's minimum.
B.18: What should you do this year? One: find last December thirty-first's balance, and divide it by your factor from the I R S table. Two: if this is your first year, decide now whether to avoid taking two distributions next year. Three: if you give to charity, ask your I R A company about a Q C D, and finish it before December thirty-first. Four: choose your withholding with Form W four R. Do these four, and April holds no surprises.
B.19: One: your minimum is last year's balance divided by the factor, and Walter's is thirty-two thousand five hundred twenty dollars. Two: your first distribution can wait until April first, but then you take two in one year. Three: missing it costs twenty-five percent, or ten percent if you fix it in time. Four: a distribution can make up to eighty-five percent of your Social Security taxable. Five: a Q C D can cut that, and it saved Walter two thousand eighty-nine dollars.
B.20: If this helped, send it to one person over seventy who has an I R A. And tell me in the comments: do you give to charity, and has anyone ever told you about a Q C D?
